title: Health Professions Education: Accelerating Innovation Through Technology
venue: Blue Ridge Academic Health Group Report 17
extended_summary:
This Blue Ridge Academic Health Group report addresses how academic health centers and health professional schools can respond to two converging forces: the need for major reform in health professions education and the rapid expansion of online learning, open educational resources, and learning platforms. The report asks how technology can help institutions move toward a more flexible, competency-based, cost-conscious, and learner-centered educational model.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the paper surveys emerging practices and institutional initiatives in medical and health professions education, including flipped classrooms, learning management systems, open courseware, MOOCs, virtual patients, simulations, and e-portfolios. It highlights examples from the University of Michigan, Stanford, New York University, Johns Hopkins, and others to illustrate how technology is being used to support continuous learning, competency tracking, interactive learning, and broader access to educational content.

The report focuses primarily on undergraduate and professional health education in the United States. Its main conclusion is that technology offers meaningful opportunities to improve flexibility, reach, and efficiency, but that the evidence base was still limited in 2012–2013. The authors therefore argue for careful implementation, institutional capacity-building, and a stronger research agenda to evaluate whether these approaches truly improve learning outcomes and competency development.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a 2013 policy/report article describing online learning trends and citing Khan Academy as an example; it does not present a primary empirical study of Khanmigo or any K-12 science learning intervention. There is no rigorous experimental or quasi-experimental methodology in the paper itself.
impact_tier_rationale: No direct outcome data are reported for K-12 science achievement, conceptual understanding, reasoning, vocabulary, inquiry skills, retention, engagement, or assignment performance. The paper only offers conceptual discussion and illustrative examples, so no measurable impact can be attributed.

interventions.use_case: Khan Academy-style mastery-based platform that tracks student progress, recommends new topics after mastery, and provides problem sets for K-12 math and science learners
